title: I made my first Zelda-inspired open-world game in two days. Here’s what I learned.
author: Meowmeowliz
selftext:
Hey everyone!

I have no game dev experience, but I’ve been trying different AI tools and workflows for a while. Finally decided to try making an open-world game and spent pretty much two full days doing nothing else.

It’s called Glimmerwild. I’m a big Zelda fan, so the inspiration is probably obvious. It’s still a prototype, but you can climb, glide, swim, cook, shoot arrows, and fight. Being able to run around in it for the first time was pretty cool.😄

**My Workflow** 

I used ChatGPT and Plan mode in Wanaka Studio to work out the initial prompt, then made reference images with GPT Image 2 and Nano Banana.   
I uploaded those to Wanaka Studio as visual references, entered the prompt, and started building.

The terrain, 3D model generation, coding, rigging, sound, and debugging all in Wanaka. It uses Three.js for rendering, so I didn’t switch tool.

The AI handled the code. I mostly gave directions, checked the results, and asked for changes. Once it was playable, it became a lot of testing, taking screenshots, and going back and forth with the AI.

**Here’s a few things I figured out along the way**  
**Hope it helps!**

**1. Build the world first, then add gameplay**  
I got the world built and made sure I was happy with the overall look before adding combat, climbing, gliding, cooking, and the rest. Doing it in stages also made it easier to figure out which addition had caused a problem.

**2. Screenshots worked better than long explanations.**  
When something looked wrong, I’d take a screenshot and add a quick note, like “the grass is floating on this slope” or “there’s a seam along the shore.” It saved a lot of explaining, and the AI could see exactly where the problem was.

**3. Use reference images to keep the art style consistent.**  
I found it hard to get a consistent look just by describing it. Giving the AI references helped more. For the UI, I used examples of parchment panels, brush-style headings, and teal item frames, then asked it to use the same style across the main menu, dialogue, and inventory.

It also helped to say what I **didn’t** want. My little companion was inspired by Navi, and I had to explicitly add, “Don’t make it a butterfly.”

**4. When a problem is hard to fix, ask why before asking for another fix.**  
With no game dev or coding experience, I often don’t know what’s causing a problem, let alone how to solve it. So I’ll ask directly: “Why is the terrain so sharp?” or “We’ve tried fixing the floating grass several times. What’s causing it, and how would you fix it?”  
Having the AI explain the cause and suggest an approach before making changes worked better than repeatedly saying “try again.” It gave us something more specific to work on.

**5. Don’t ask the AI to change too much at once.**  
When I had a long list of changes, it helped to pick out the most important ones and tackle those first. Throwing the whole list at the AI didn’t magically make the game better.

**8. Let someone else play before calling it done.**  
By the end, I honestly thought it was looking pretty good. Then my friends found camera clipping, weird hand movements when drawing the bow, and weapons that didn’t move properly with the character. I’d got used to testing in a certain way. They went places and tried things I hadn’t, which caught a lot of what I’d missed.

Still plenty to fix, but I’m happy I finally gave it a shot. Would love to hear what you think, especially about the look of the world！

replies.author: Meowmeowliz
replies.body:
That’s a fair point, and I could have explained it more clearly. Since this was an open-world project, I found it helpful to build a rough version of the larger environment first, so I could establish the scale, atmosphere, and visual direction.

From my own testing, adding the gameplay mechanics on top of that foundation made the process feel clearer and smoother. When I asked the AI to handle the environment and several mechanics at the same time, different issues sometimes became tangled together and were harder to track. Working in stages made it easier for me to understand what had changed and where a new problem came from.

That said, this is just the workflow that worked for me. Different kinds of games may benefit from a different order.

replies.author: Meowmeowliz
replies.body:
I get that these tips may feel basic if you already have more experience. I started with zero coding or game dev experience, and learned them by spending time and tokens, making mistakes, and building something playable. They’re the things I now reuse most, so I wanted to share them in case someone else finds them helpful. Everyone has to learn the basics somewhere.

It’s a playable prototype of an open-world game. You can already explore the world and try the main mechanics, but it obviously still needs more development and polish. I’m proud of what I managed to build in two days, but I wasn’t trying to suggest that it’s a finished game.

Anyway, I’m still learning and just wanted to share the process as I go.
